items.readable_text:
Content:
In this topic, we'll study phase portraits of linear systems
[MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]
where the eigenvalues of a [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix [MATH: A] are
[MATH: \lambda_{1,2}=a\pm b\text{i},
\qquad b\neq 0.]

Content:
Let [MATH: \mathbf{v}=\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{q}\text{i},] where [MATH: \mathbf{p},\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^2,] be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda = a + b\text{i}.]

Content:
Then, a complex solution of the system is given by
[MATH: \mathbf{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) = \mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}.]

Content:
Using Euler's formula, we obtain
[MATH: x_{complex}(t)|= ve^{(a + b\textrm{i})t}; = e^{at}(\cos (bt) + \textrm{i}\sin (bt))(p + q\textrm{i}); = e^{at}(\cos (bt)p − \sin (bt)q) + \textrm{i}e^{at}(\sin (bt)p + \cos (bt)q).]

Content:
Therefore, the general solution of the system is
[MATH: \mathbf{x}(t) =
c_1 e^{at}\big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big) +
c_2 e^{at}\big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big).]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \cos(bt)] and [MATH: \sin(bt)] are bounded, so the factor [MATH: e^{at}] controls the long-term behavior:

Content:
- If [MATH: a>0,] then [MATH: e^{at}\to\infty] as [MATH: t\to\infty.] So, trajectories are unbounded, and we have a spiral that is traversed toward infinity as [MATH: t \to \infty.]
- If [MATH: a<0,] then [MATH: e^{at}\to 0] as [MATH: t\to\infty.] So, trajectories approach the origin, and we have a spiral that is traversed toward the origin as [MATH: t \to \infty.]
- If [MATH: a=0,] then [MATH: e^{at}=1] for all [MATH: t.] So, trajectories are bounded, and we have an ellipse.

Content:
Let's see some concrete examples.

Therefore, the general solution of the system is [MATH: \textbf{x}(t) = c_1 e^{at}\big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big) + c_2 e^{at}\big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big),] where the parts [MATH: \big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big)] and [MATH: \big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big)] are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is unbounded, representing a spiral that is traversed counterclockwise. Thus, we must have [MATH: a \neq 0.]

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward the origin.

Hence, to insure that [MATH: e^{at} \to 0,] we require [MATH: a < 0.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this topic, we'll study phase portraits of linear systems
[MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]
where the eigenvalues of a [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix [MATH: A] are
[MATH: \lambda_{1,2}=a\pm b\text{i},
\qquad b\neq 0.]

Content:
Let [MATH: \mathbf{v}=\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{q}\text{i},] where [MATH: \mathbf{p},\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^2,] be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda = a + b\text{i}.]

Content:
Then, a complex solution of the system is given by
[MATH: \mathbf{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) = \mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}.]

Content:
Using Euler's formula, we obtain
[MATH: x_{complex}(t)|= ve^{(a + b\textrm{i})t}; = e^{at}(\cos (bt) + \textrm{i}\sin (bt))(p + q\textrm{i}); = e^{at}(\cos (bt)p − \sin (bt)q) + \textrm{i}e^{at}(\sin (bt)p + \cos (bt)q).]

Content:
Therefore, the general solution of the system is
[MATH: \mathbf{x}(t) =
c_1 e^{at}\big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big) +
c_2 e^{at}\big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big).]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \cos(bt)] and [MATH: \sin(bt)] are bounded, so the factor [MATH: e^{at}] controls the long-term behavior:

Content:
- If [MATH: a>0,] then [MATH: e^{at}\to\infty] as [MATH: t\to\infty.] So, trajectories are unbounded, and we have a spiral that is traversed toward infinity as [MATH: t \to \infty.]
- If [MATH: a<0,] then [MATH: e^{at}\to 0] as [MATH: t\to\infty.] So, trajectories approach the origin, and we have a spiral that is traversed toward the origin as [MATH: t \to \infty.]
- If [MATH: a=0,] then [MATH: e^{at}=1] for all [MATH: t.] So, trajectories are bounded, and we have an ellipse.

Content:
Let's see some concrete examples.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Systems With Complex Eigenvalues

Content:
Consider the system of linear differential equations below.
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = (1)/(2)x(t) − 4y(t); y^{′}(t) = 4x(t) + (1)/(2)y(t)]
The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are [MATH: \lambda_{1,2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\pm4\text{i},] for which the corresponding eigenvectors are [MATH: \mathbf{v}_{1,2} = [\pm \text{i}, 1]^T,] respectively. Given that the general solution of the system is
[MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]
we are interested in sketching the phase portrait of the system of differential equations given above.

Content:
If we set [MATH: c_1 = 1] and [MATH: c_2 = 0] in the general solution of the system, we obtain the particular solution:
[MATH: {x = e^{t/2}\cos (4t); y = e^{t/2}\sin (4t)]

Content:
Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

Content:
| [MATH: t] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{16}] | [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{8}] |
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 0.78] | [MATH: 0] |
| [MATH: y] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 0.78] | [MATH: 1.22] |

Content:
Let's sketch this solution in the phase space.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f61bc7723bc855463e9d8018cd58eab0]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: |\sin(4t)| \leq 1] and [MATH: |\cos(4t)| \leq 1,] but [MATH: e^{t/2} \to \infty] as [MATH: t \to \infty.] Thus, the obtained curve is unbounded. So, we have a spiral that is traversed counterclockwise.

Content:
Again, since [MATH: e^{t/2} \to \infty] as [MATH: t \to \infty,] the spiral is traversed toward infinity as [MATH: t \to \infty.]

Content:
The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

- If [MATH: a<0,] we have a stable spiral (sink).

Item 10 — Example: Classifying Systems of Linear Differential Equations With Complex Eigenvalues

Example Prompt:
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = − 2y(t); y^{′}(t) = 2x(t)]
Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are [MATH: \lambda=\pm2\text{i}.] Provide an interpretation of the equilibrium point (origin) for the system of differential equations given above.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: \mathbf{v}=\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{q}\text{i},] where [MATH: \mathbf{p},\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^2,] be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda = a + b\text{i}.]

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by
[MATH: \mathbf{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) = \mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}.]

Using Euler's formula, we obtain
[MATH: x_{complex}(t)|= ve^{(a + b\textrm{i})t}; = e^{at}(\cos (bt) + \textrm{i}\sin (bt))(p + q\textrm{i}); = e^{at}(\cos (bt)p − \sin (bt)q) + \textrm{i}e^{at}(\sin (bt)p + \cos (bt)q).]

Therefore, the general solution of the system is
[MATH: \textbf{x}(t) =
c_1 e^{at}\big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big) +
c_2 e^{at}\big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big),]
where the parts [MATH: \big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big)] and [MATH: \big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big)] are bounded.

Now, notice that [MATH: a = \text{Re}(\lambda) = 0] and [MATH: e^{at} = e^{0\cdot t} = 1] for all [MATH: t.] Thus, we have an ellipse that curves around the origin.

Therefore, since [MATH: \text{Re}(\lambda) = 0,] the equilibrium point (origin) is a center.
